cue: Red turns dark, and the picture runs slowly, then jumps ahead.

BEE.note: their green drawn as red, their blue as green; ultraviolet goes to blue

rows: Most insects see less than a sixtieth as much detail as people do.
Bees have no colour-sensing cells for red, so red flowers and objects look dark to them.
In bright light, a honeybee can see a light flicker up to 200 times a second, where people stop at about 60. This view runs slowly and then jumps ahead to suggest the difference.
Bees can see ultraviolet light, which people can’t. Phone cameras capture very little of it, so the blue in this view stands in for it.
A bee sees green, blue and ultraviolet. Since a screen can’t show ultraviolet, this view moves every colour over by one: a bee’s green appears as red, its blue as green, and its ultraviolet as blue.

rows: Bumblebees of the species Bombus impatiens separate stripes only as fine as 0.35 cycles per degree, and honeybees reach about 0.26 to 0.36. You very likely see less than a hundredth of the detail a human reads on an eye chart.

Honeybees have an ultraviolet receptor near 344 nanometers, a bumblebee has a green receptor near 540, and a red mason bee has a blue receptor near 436. You very likely have the same three kinds, so you see ultraviolet, blue and green and red light looks dark to you.
Bees are said to see about 300 degrees across the body plane, and a honeybee about 270. You very likely take in almost the whole circle around you, with the finest detail straight ahead.

A bumblebee's eye follows flicker up to about 130 times a second, a free-flying honeybee's color vision about 100, and a honeybee in bright light about 200. You very likely catch changes that a human, at 60, blurs together.
In a forager honeybee the front of each eye is the sharpest part, with facets as little as 1.3 degrees apart. Toward the sides they sit farther apart.
If you are a honeybee, you read the pattern of polarized light in the sky as a compass, using ultraviolet receptors at the top rim of your eye. Bumblebees have such receptors too.

Nobody has measured how quickly sharpness fades from the front of a worker's eye to its edge, or how much of what you see as blue reads to you as ultraviolet. A compound eye has no pupil, and no record describes one.

On this trial the colours come from the honeybee's three measured receptor classes, ultraviolet in the bluest slot. The camera's colours and the ultraviolet guess are the app's.
A tap keeps the last moment and plays it three times slower, as a faster eye might have time for it. The ratio is the app's guess.

Many insects see the direction in which sky light is polarized, strongest in a band 90 degrees from the sun, and steer by it. With &draw=polar and the motion sensors on, fine strokes show that band from the time, the date and the phone's heading. The latitude is taken as 35 degrees north, and the drawing is the app's.

uvBlue.note: the matrix's fourth column carries the ultraviolet

fov.note: between the 300 degrees given for bees and the 270 given for the honeybee

cpd.note: measured with gratings in one bumblebee species and used for every bee; honeybee figures run from 0.25 to 0.36

topoA.note: the front of the eye is sharpest, but no record gives a ratio for a worker

fall.note: how fast sharpness drops toward the edge is the app's choice

pupil.note: a compound eye has no pupil; no record describes one

rate.note: 60 divided by 130 hertz; records for bees run from 100 to 200 hertz

polar.note: how strongly the polarized band of sky is drawn
